981.title: John Baptist de La Salle (7 April)
981.hook: a wealthy canon who gave up his comfort to start free schools for poor boys
981.howItsDone: Catholics keep John Baptist de La Salle's memorial on 7 April; the De La Salle Brothers and their schools honor him as their founder.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vincent Ferrer, the Dominican whose pulpit was the road. Your line was walking preacher. Where did your feet do the talking? Day nine hundred eighty-one.

A young priest in Reims has the kind of life people envy. A rich family, a fine house, a seat as a canon at the cathedral, good dinners, good books. Then he agrees to help a man who wants to open schools for poor boys, the kind who spend their days in the street. He'll just give a bit of advice. Then he'll find the teachers a place to stay. Then, because they're struggling, he invites them to eat at his own table. His family is appalled. These men are rough, untrained, poorly paid. He keeps saying yes, one small step at a time. Today, how a favor became a life.
screen: `A CANON WITH AN ENVIABLE LIFE.` → `JUST A LITTLE HELP.` → `TEACHERS AT HIS TABLE.`

segments.voice: John Baptist de La Salle later said that if he had known where those first steps would lead, he might never have taken them. But he took them. Step by step, he brought the teachers into his own house to live. Then he gave up his post at the cathedral. Then, tradition says, during a time of hunger, he gave away his family fortune to the poor, so that he would stand where his teachers stood, with nothing to fall back on. Out of that household came a community: the Brothers of the Christian Schools. They were not priests. They were laymen who made vows and gave their lives to one thing, teaching poor children, for free. La Salle changed how the teaching was done. Lessons in the children's own language, French, instead of Latin. Children grouped by what they knew, and taught together, not one at a time while the rest waited. And training for the teachers themselves, so that a teacher was not just whoever could be found, but someone formed for the work. He also wrote for his brothers about the inner side of teaching: that a classroom is a place where God is present, and that the brothers should recognize Jesus in the poor children in front of them. The prophet Daniel has a line about teachers, in the Douay-Rheims: "they that instruct many to justice, as stars for all eternity." The Church later named La Salle patron of teachers. It began with a few hungry teachers at his table.
screen: `ONE SMALL STEP AT A TIME.` · `HE GAVE UP HIS POST AND HIS FORTUNE.` · `BROTHERS WHO TAUGHT POOR CHILDREN FREE.` · `A NEW WAY TO RUN A CLASSROOM.` · then, large: `AS STARS FOR ALL ETERNITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a teacher. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one teacher who changed something for you. A schoolteacher, a coach, a grandparent at a kitchen table, a boss who took time to show you how. See their face. Remember one specific thing they did: a sentence, a second chance, a moment they didn't give up. Now plan the thank-you: a message, a card, a call, or, if they've died, a word said to someone who knew them. If you pray, you can thank God for them. If you don't, just let the gratitude be real. The bell holds the time.
John Baptist de La Salle. A canon of Reims who gave up his comfort and fortune to found brothers who taught poor children for free.
screen: `JOHN BAPTIST DE LA SALLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: patron of teachers. Today, send your thank-you, and be patient with one person who is learning something from you. Day nine hundred eighty-one.

982.title: Stanislaus (11 April)
982.hook: a bishop of Kraków killed by the king he had rebuked
982.howItsDone: Catholics keep Stanislaus's memorial on 11 April; in Poland his feast is kept in May with a procession in Kraków, carrying his relics from Wawel Cathedral to the church on the Skałka hill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, John Baptist de La Salle, who turned a favor into free schools for poor boys. Your line was patron of teachers. Did your thank-you reach its teacher? Day nine hundred eighty-two.

A small church on a hill outside Kraków. A bishop is at the altar, saying Mass. The door opens, and armed men come in, sent by the king. According to the tradition, they can't bring themselves to touch him. So the king walks in himself, and strikes the bishop down at the altar. That is how the story is told in Poland. The bishop's name was Stanislaus. The king's was Bolesław. And between them stood a question that keeps coming back: what happens when a pastor tells a powerful man no?
screen: `A BISHOP AT THE ALTAR.` → `THE KING STRIKES HIM DOWN.` → `WHEN A PASTOR TELLS POWER NO.`

segments.voice: Start with honesty about the sources, because they disagree. An early Polish chronicle is brief and harsh about him, and calls the bishop a traitor. A later chronicler, a bishop of Kraków himself, tells it the other way: Stanislaus rebuked the king for cruelty and for his sins, the king would not listen, and the bishop finally cut him off from the Church. Historians still argue about what really happened between them. The sources do agree on the ending. The king had the bishop killed, and soon afterward the king himself was driven from his throne and died in exile. Tradition adds more. Stories grew of a dead man raised to testify for the bishop in a land dispute, and of the bishop's scattered body growing whole again, which Poles later read as a picture of their divided country one day becoming one. The Church named Stanislaus a saint, and he became a patron of Poland. His story echoes an older one. In the Gospel of Mark, John the Baptist tells King Herod, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." John lost his head for that sentence. Speaking plainly to a king is a risk. In Polish memory, Stanislaus became a sign that the Church's voice belongs to the people, not to the throne. A later bishop of Kraków, Karol Wojtyła, who became Pope John Paul the Second, kept returning to him. The bishop of Kraków is a title with a memory.
screen: `THE SOURCES DISAGREE.` · `HE REBUKED THE KING.` · `THE KING KILLED HIM, THEN LOST HIS THRONE.` · `A SIGN FOR A DIVIDED COUNTRY.` · then, large: `IT IS NOT LAWFUL FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold Poland. Settle, and breathe. Bring Poland to mind as people, not a map. A grandmother in Kraków walking to morning Mass. A family who left and a family who stayed. Polish neighbors, coworkers or friends where you live. Hold the country's long memory of being divided, and whatever it carries today. If you pray, you can pray for Poland, perhaps with the Hail Mary or the Our Father. If you don't, simply hold its people in mind with good will. The bell holds the time.
Stanislaus. A bishop of Kraków killed at the king's order after he rebuked him, honored as a patron of Poland.
Your line: the bishop of kraków. Today, when you hear a story told only one way, look for the other telling before you decide. Day nine hundred eighty-two.

983.title: George (23 April)
983.hook: a soldier-martyr whose dragon is a legend, patron of England and other lands
983.howItsDone: Catholics keep Saint George's optional memorial on 23 April; in England it is a feast, and Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Christians honor him as a great martyr with icons of the rider and the dragon.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stanislaus, struck down after he told a king no. Your line was the bishop of kraków. Did you find the other telling of a story? Day nine hundred eighty-three.

A red cross on a white field, flying over a stadium in England. A knight on a horse, spearing a dragon, on a gold coin, a church window, a pub sign. A painted icon in an Orthodox church, the same young rider, the same twisting beast under his hooves. The man in all of them is George. Yet the dragon is the part tradition added later. Behind the horse and the spear stands a much plainer story: a soldier, and a choice. Today, the man under the legend.
screen: `A RED CROSS, A KNIGHT, A DRAGON.` → `THE DRAGON CAME LATER.` → `A SOLDIER, AND A CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Here is what tradition holds about George himself. He was a soldier in the Roman army in the east, a Christian, at a time when an emperor ordered Christians to sacrifice to the gods. George would not. He was tortured and put to death, and Christians began to honor his grave. Beyond that, the details are thin, and the Church is frank about it. An early Church decree, long credited to a pope, counted him among saints whose names people rightly honor but whose deeds are known only to God. Then the dragon. In a medieval collection of saints' lives called the Golden Legend, a dragon terrorizes a city, demanding victims, until the lot falls on the king's daughter. George rides up, wounds the beast in the name of Christ, and the princess leads it into the city on her own sash. The people ask for baptism. It's a legend, and a beloved one, told and painted across Europe and the Christian East. The Church holds both pieces: the martyr, whose feast the Church keeps, and the legend, which is free to be what it is, a picture. Saint Paul gives the same picture without the scales. In the Douay-Rheims: "Put you on the armour of God, that you may be able to stand against the deceits of the devil." The dragon in the story stands for evil. The real George's dragon was an order he would not obey. England, Georgia, Catalonia and other places took him as patron. The legend gave him a beast. The refusal is the part the oldest tellings already hold.
screen: `A SOLDIER WHO WOULD NOT SACRIFICE.` · `HIS DEEDS KNOWN ONLY TO GOD.` · `THE DRAGON: A MEDIEVAL LEGEND.` · `HIS REAL DRAGON WAS AN ORDER.` · then, large: `PUT YOU ON THE ARMOUR OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: face one dragon. Settle, and breathe. Name one dragon in your own life. Not a monster, maybe. A habit that eats your evenings. A fear you feed to keep it quiet. A demand you keep giving in to. A conversation you keep dodging. Look at it plainly, the way George looked at the order he would not obey. You don't need to slay it today. Just name it, and choose one small first move against it. If you pray, you can ask for courage, perhaps with the Our Father's line, deliver us from evil. If you don't, just hold your one move steady. The bell holds the time.
George. A soldier martyred for refusing to sacrifice to the gods, whose dragon is a medieval legend, honored as patron of England and other places.
Your line: slay the dragon. Today, make your one small first move against the dragon you named. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

984.title: Mark (25 April)
984.hook: the evangelist behind the Gospel that starts with a voice in the desert; his symbol is the lion
984.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mark the Evangelist on 25 April, reading from his Gospel at Mass; in Venice, where tradition says his relics rest, his day is a great civic and church feast.

segments.voice: Yesterday, George, the soldier under the dragon legend. Your line was slay the dragon. What was your first small move? Day nine hundred eighty-four.

No manger. No angels. No family tree. One sentence of title, and then a shout from the wilderness. That's how the Gospel of Mark begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." A few lines later, a voice crying in the desert, John the Baptist in camel's hair, and Jesus already walking down to the river. Some readers call it the Gospel in a hurry. Today, the man the Church remembers as its writer, and why his sign is a lion.
screen: `NO MANGER, NO ANGELS.` → `A SHOUT FROM THE WILDERNESS.` → `THE GOSPEL IN A HURRY.`

segments.voice: Who was Mark? The Gospel itself never says. Tradition fills in the name. An early bishop, Papias, wrote that Mark had been Peter's interpreter, and set down what Peter remembered of the Lord's words and deeds. Tradition also links him with the John Mark of the Acts of the Apostles, whose mother's house in Jerusalem was a place where the believers gathered, and who set out with Paul and Barnabas, then turned back partway. Paul refused to take him on the next journey, and Paul and Barnabas split over it. Yet in a later letter Paul asks for Mark to be brought to him, because he is useful. A young man who failed once, and was trusted again. Some readers even wonder whether the young man in Mark's own Gospel, who runs off naked from Gethsemane when Jesus is arrested, is the writer quietly signing his work. Nobody can know. Now the lion. Christians long ago matched the four Gospel writers with the four living creatures in Ezekiel and Revelation: a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. Saint Jerome gave Mark the lion, because his Gospel opens with a voice roaring in the wilderness. In the Douay-Rheims: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." Venice later took Mark as its patron, and his winged lion still stands over the city. A short Gospel, a loud beginning, and a writer who was given a second chance.
screen: `THE GOSPEL NEVER NAMES ITS WRITER.` · `PETER'S INTERPRETER, TRADITION SAYS.` · `JOHN MARK: FAILED ONCE, TRUSTED AGAIN.` · `A LION FOR A ROARING VOICE.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one chapter of Mark. Settle, and breathe. If you have a Bible or an app nearby, open to Mark, chapter one. If not, just plan when you'll do it today. Chapter one is a short read. As you read, notice the pace. Jesus is always on the move: the river, the desert, the lake, a house full of people, a lonely place before dawn. Let the speed pull you along. If you pray, you can ask to hear it as if for the first time. If you don't, simply read it as a story. The bell holds the time.
Mark. The evangelist the Church names as writer of the Gospel that opens with a voice in the desert, marked by the lion.
Your line: the lion. Today, read Mark chapter one, and see how many places Jesus goes before it ends. Day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: Zita (27 April)
985.hook: a housemaid in Lucca who served one household all her working life, patron of domestic workers
985.howItsDone: Zita is remembered on 27 April, especially in Lucca, where on her day people bring flowers to the church of San Frediano; domestic workers and those who look after homes have taken her as their patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mark, the evangelist whose Gospel opens with a voice in the desert. Your line was the lion. How many places did Jesus go in chapter one? Day nine hundred eighty-five.

Who cleaned the house you grew up in? Maybe a parent, after a full shift. Maybe a grandmother. Maybe a woman who came on Thursdays and whose last name nobody in the family ever learned. Housework is the work that is noticed mainly when it isn't done. Nobody gives speeches about a clean floor. Today's saint never ran a school, never preached, never founded anything. She scrubbed floors and baked bread for one family in the Italian city of Lucca. And the city honored her as a saint. Today, Zita.
screen: `WHO CLEANED YOUR HOUSE?` → `WORK NOTICED WHEN IT ISN'T DONE.` → `A MAID IN LUCCA.`

segments.voice: Zita went to work as a servant for a wealthy family in Lucca when she was still a girl, and tradition says she stayed in that house for the rest of her life. It was not easy at first. The stories say the other servants resented her for working hard and praying often, and her employers treated her harshly. She kept working. She rose early to go to Mass, and then did the day's work well. Slowly the household changed its mind about her, until she was trusted with the running of the house. She was known for giving to the poor: her own food, and sometimes, the stories admit, the family's. One legend says that her master once stopped her as she carried bread out in her apron, and when she opened it, there were only flowers. Another says she lent her master's cloak to a freezing beggar on Christmas Eve, and a stranger brought it back. Those are legends. The steady part isn't. A servant who worked hard, prayed, and gave. Saint Paul writes to servants and masters in the letter to the Colossians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whatsoever you do, do it from the heart, as to the Lord, and not to men." Her biographers saw Zita in that sentence. In their telling, her work wasn't holy because it was impressive. It was holy because of whom she was doing it for. People in Lucca honored her, and the Church named her patron of domestic workers. Her day is a good day to notice the people whose work makes everyone else's day possible.
screen: `A SERVANT GIRL IN ONE HOUSE.` · `MASS FIRST, THEN THE DAY'S WORK.` · `BREAD FOR THE POOR, AND LEGENDS.` · `PATRON OF DOMESTIC WORKERS.` · then, large: `DO IT FROM THE HEART, AS TO THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who cleans. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who cleans a space you use. The custodian at work or school. The person who cleans the hotel room, the hospital ward, the office at night. Someone at home. If you don't know their name, notice that. Plan one real thank-you, said to their face, with their name if you can learn it. And if the person who cleans is you, notice that too: the dishes and the laundry count. If you pray, you can offer your own chores today, as Zita did. If you don't, just hold the people in mind. The bell holds the time.
Zita. A housemaid in Lucca who worked, prayed and gave to the poor, honored as patron of domestic workers.
Your line: holy in housework. Today, learn the name of one person who cleans where you go, and thank them. Day nine hundred eighty-five.

986.title: Peter Chanel (28 April)
986.hook: a quiet missionary killed on the Pacific island of Futuna, honored as the first martyr of Oceania
986.howItsDone: Catholics keep Peter Chanel's optional memorial on 28 April; it is kept with special honor in Oceania, and the Marists remember him as one of their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zita, the housemaid of Lucca who did her work as to the Lord. Your line was holy in housework. Whose name did you learn, and did you thank them? Day nine hundred eighty-six.

Not every missionary story has crowds in it. This one has a small island in the middle of the Pacific, a French priest who has learned the local language, a garden, a hut, and a handful of people interested in what he teaches. Most days, he visits the sick. He listens. Very little seems to happen. Then the son of the island's king asks to be baptized, and everything changes, fast. Today, Peter Chanel, a man whose whole mission looked small.
screen: `A SMALL ISLAND IN THE PACIFIC.` → `MOST DAYS, HE VISITS AND LISTENS.` → `THE KING'S SON ASKS FOR BAPTISM.`

segments.voice: Peter Chanel was a French priest who joined the Marists, the Society of Mary, and asked to be sent to the missions. He was sent to Futuna, an island far out in the Pacific. He learned the language. He cared for the sick, and people came to know him for his gentleness. For a long time, almost nobody asked for baptism. The island's king had welcomed the missionaries at first. But as a few islanders, and then his own son, began to turn to the new faith, the king came to see it as a threat to his authority. One morning, men sent from the king's side came to Peter's hut and killed him with clubs and an axe. Here the story turns. Tradition says that soon after his death, the people of Futuna asked for baptism, and the island became Catholic. The Church honors Peter Chanel as the first martyr of Oceania. Jesus says in the Gospel of John, in the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die, itself remaineth alone. But if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit." That's the shape of Peter's life. A seed that looked wasted. Today, Catholics in the Pacific, from Futuna to New Zealand and Australia, keep his feast. And on Futuna itself, the island where he was killed, people now keep his memory at the place where he died.
screen: `A MARIST SENT TO FUTUNA.` · `YEARS OF SMALL, QUIET WORK.` · `KILLED AFTER THE KING'S SON TURNED.` · `THE FIRST MARTYR OF OCEANIA.` · then, large: `IF IT DIE, IT BRINGETH FORTH MUCH FRUIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small island, then the whole ocean. Settle, and breathe. Start with one island, Futuna. Picture a garden, a hut, a sick neighbor being visited. Then let the picture widen: Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, cities from Auckland to Manila. Fishing families, children walking to school, churches singing in island languages, coasts facing rising seas. If you know someone from the Pacific, start with their face instead. If you pray, you can pray for the peoples of the Pacific. If you don't, let the picture stay wide for the length of the bell. The bell holds the time.
Peter Chanel. A Marist missionary who served quietly on Futuna, was killed there, and is honored by the Church as the first martyr of Oceania.
Your line: first of oceania. Today, find Futuna on a map, and read one thing about the people who live there now. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

987.title: Joseph the Worker (1 May)
987.hook: the carpenter of Nazareth, kept on the first of May, the day set aside for workers
987.howItsDone: On 1 May the Catholic calendar keeps an optional memorial of Saint Joseph the Worker; Catholics often pray for workers and the unemployed, and some parishes bless tools or hold Masses for labor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter Chanel, the quiet missionary killed on Futuna. Your line was first of Oceania. Who in the Pacific did you hold in prayer, or in mind? Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

A workbench. Shavings curled on the floor. A plane, a saw, a few nails in a dish. On the first of May, a day when marchers in cities carry banners for workers, the Catholic calendar sets this bench in the middle of the church. Not a throne. Not a battlefield. A shop in a small town. This week we've walked with a teacher, a bishop, a soldier, an evangelist, a housemaid and a missionary. Today the saints' calendar turns into May, and it opens with a man whose hands smelled of wood. Today, Joseph the Worker.
screen: `A WORKBENCH.` → `THE FIRST OF MAY.` → `A SHOP IN A SMALL TOWN.`

segments.voice: The Gospels say almost nothing about Joseph's job. It comes up once, and not as praise. Jesus is teaching in his home town, and the neighbors can't get past where he comes from. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter's son?" The Greek word behind carpenter, tektōn, can mean someone who works in wood, or more widely a builder or craftsman. Either way, the town is saying: we know this family. They work with their hands, like us. Here's the turn. The feast takes that sneer and makes it the whole point. The Son of God, as they believe him to be, grew up in a working house. He learned a trade beside Joseph. For the years the Gospels skip, tradition pictures him simply at work. So the feast makes a quiet claim: ordinary labor is not time away from God. Sanding a door, stocking a shelf, answering the same email again. The Church gave Joseph a feast on the workers' day so that the day would have a saint in it. Catholics hold this feast in more than one way. Some keep it as a prayer for their own work, asking Joseph to help them do it honestly. Others keep it for the people who can't find work at all, or who work in danger, or for too little. And some simply notice that the Gospels never record a single word spoken by Joseph. He is remembered for what he did, not what he said. A silent man at a bench, and a whole feast for the work of his hands.

If you pray, you can ask Saint Joseph to stand beside them at the next door they knock on. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and the dignity of what their hands can do. The bell holds the time.
Joseph the Worker. The carpenter of Nazareth, kept on the first of May, whose silent work Catholics honor as holy.
